opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I get a lot, especially now, given how things turned out.

When I was at OpenAI, it was a very different place from what it is today. It was small, with a handful of researchers trying ideas, and the GPT work came out of exploring whether generative pre-training on lots of unlabeled text could give you representations that transfer to many downstream tasks. It was exciting, but nobody was sure it would become what it did.

I had always planned an academic career. During my PhD at MIT I really enjoyed mentoring students and having the freedom to pick problems based on curiosity rather than a product roadmap. The Princeton offer was a chance to build a group around the questions I cared about most: how language connects to action, how agents can use language to learn and reason in interactive environments. That felt like a long-term research agenda that suited a university.

There's also something about training students that compounds. A paper is one contribution, but if you help a few dozen people become independent researchers, they go on to do things you'd never have thought of. That's been one of the most rewarding parts.

Did I think about the counterfactual once GPT-3, ChatGPT and everything after happened? Of course, it's hard not to. But academia has let me work across that boundary. We still collaborate with industry, and my students have worked on things like language agents, benchmarks for coding and web tasks, and ways to evaluate these systems. Academia plays a different role now. We can't always train the biggest models, but we can ask questions industry has less incentive to ask, around evaluation, understanding, and new directions that aren't yet commercially obvious.

So I don't see it as choosing one over the other. It was choosing the setting where I thought I could contribute most over the long run, and I'm still happy with that choice.

r001.rationale: He says academia gave him freedom to choose curiosity-driven problems and build a group around several research questions, and that Princeton was the setting where he could contribute most over the long run.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a question I get a lot, and honestly it wasn't an easy call. I was at OpenAI during a pretty special window. We were working on the first GPT paper, and you could feel that something was shifting in how language models were going to work. So leaving right as that was taking off looked a little strange from the outside.

But a few things pulled me toward academia. The first is that I really like the freedom to pick problems based on curiosity rather than on what a roadmap needs this quarter. In a lab like OpenAI, even back then, the big bets were set at the org level, and you work within that. At a university I can decide that I want to spend three years on, say, how agents learn from interaction in text environments, or how to ground language in action, even if nobody can tell you yet whether it's going to be commercially useful.

The second thing is students. I genuinely enjoy mentoring. Watching a PhD student go from not knowing what a good research question looks like to running their own agenda is one of the most rewarding things I've done. You don't get that in the same way in industry.

And the third is honestly a bit of a bet on where the interesting questions would end up. I had a sense that scaling was going to be done really well by the big labs, and that the harder, less glamorous questions about reasoning, grounding, interaction, and evaluation would benefit from people who weren't on the hook for shipping. Princeton gave me the resources and the colleagues to go after those.

I'll say the tradeoffs are real. Compute is harder to come by, and you can't just spin up a few hundred GPUs for an idea. But that constraint has also pushed my group toward work where the insight matters more than the scale, and I think that's turned out to be a healthy place to be. And I've kept one foot in industry through collaborations, so it's never felt like a clean break so much as a change in what I get to prioritize.

r001.rationale: The response presents academic freedom as the first reason: it says he could choose problems based on curiosity and pursue varied directions, with examples. This identifies exploring research directions as his leading reason for choosing Princeton.

Princeton offered a chance to bring those two things together: doing research and building a group through teaching and mentorship.
